q2: WITH alias1 AS ( SELECT t2.c1 AS beer, MIN(t5.c3) AS min_price FROM t2 LEFT JOIN t5 ON t2.c1 = t5.c2 GROUP BY t2.c1 ), alias2 AS ( SELECT t5.c2 AS beer, t5.c3 AS price, t5.c1 AS bar FROM t5 JOIN alias1 ON t5.c2 = alias1.beer AND t5.c3 = alias1.min_price ) SELECT alias1.beer, alias1.min_price AS price, alias2.bar FROM alias1 LEFT JOIN alias2 ON alias1.beer = alias2.beer UNION ALL SELECT t2.c1 AS beer, NULL AS price, NULL AS bar FROM t2 WHERE t2.c1 NOT IN ( SELECT DISTINCT t5.c2 FROM t5 ) ORDER BY beer;
explanation: Both queries try to return, for each beer in t2, the minimum price from t5 (and the bar that offered that price). In Q1 the computation is done by joining t2 with a subquery (computed solely from t5) so that even beers with no t5 row will produce one row (with nulls) while beers with matching rows yield one (or multiple matching) row(s). In Q2, however, the CTE alias1 computes the beer and its min_price using a LEFT JOIN and GROUP BY so that beers with no t5 row get a row with a null min_price. Then, Q2’s second part (the UNION ALL) explicitly selects beers from t2 that do not appear in t5, thereby causing beers with no matching t5 row to appear twice (once from the CTE join output and once from the second part). Thus, when a beer in t2 has no corresponding row in t5, Q1 returns one row (beer, null, null) while Q2 returns two identical rows.
